units.title: Unit 51 — Change
learningObjectives: Distinguish scale and impact in phrases describing minor, profound and far-reaching changes.
Use change as a noun and verb with conventional collocations in reports and conversation.
Describe gradual shifts, economic trends and personal transformations precisely.
Avoid frequent unnatural pairings with data, statistics and intensifying adverbs.

items.example: The neighbourhood has seen dramatic changes since the new railway opened.
items.note: Dramatic changes are highly noticeable or striking; the phrase does not necessarily imply a negative outcome.

items.example: The revised charter introduced fundamental changes to the organisation’s voting rules.
items.note: Fundamental changes affect the basic structure or principles rather than surface details.

items.example: Moving production overseas would represent a radical change in strategy.
items.note: A radical change marks a far-reaching departure from the previous approach.

items.example: The incoming director announced sweeping changes across all regional offices.
items.note: Sweeping changes affect many parts of a system; sweeping normally modifies changes, not the verb change.

items.example: We usually cook at home, but trying the new café would make a change.
items.note: Make a change can mean do something refreshingly different from the usual routine.

items.example: Please make necessary changes to the draft before submitting it.
items.note: Make changes means alter something; the adjective necessary identifies revisions that are required.

items.example: The hospital plans to implement changes to its appointment system in January.
items.note: Implement changes means put already decided changes into practice, rather than merely propose them.

items.example: Significant changes came about after the residents organised a local campaign.
items.note: Come about explains that changes happened, often with attention to the reason or process.

items.example: Several changes took place while the museum was closed for renovation.
items.note: Take place is a relatively formal way of saying that events or changes happened.

items.example: Cycling to work instead of driving would make a nice change.
items.note: The adjective nice explicitly evaluates the departure from routine as pleasant.

items.section: B · Changing and remaining the same
items.example: The coastline could change dramatically if storms become more frequent.
items.note: Dramatically describes the large and noticeable extent of a change, not how quickly it happens.

items.section: B · Changing and remaining the same
items.example: The discovery may fundamentally change how researchers approach the question.
items.note: Fundamentally emphasises a change in the underlying nature of something.

items.section: B · Changing and remaining the same
items.example: The team radically changed its design after the first field trial.
items.note: Radically highlights an extreme departure from previous practice; radically change is a natural verb pairing.

items.section: B · Changing and remaining the same
items.example: Over several decades, the riverbank changed imperceptibly as fine sediment accumulated.
items.note: Imperceptibly means so gradually or subtly that the change is difficult to notice.

items.pt: mudar a ponto de ficar irreconhecível
items.section: B · Changing and remaining the same
items.example: The old warehouse changed beyond recognition after the restoration.
items.note: Beyond recognition means the result looks so different that the original is difficult to identify.

items.section: B · Changing and remaining the same
items.example: After becoming a father, Rafael returned from leave a changed man.
items.note: Calling someone a changed man normally conveys approval of a positive personal transformation.

items.section: B · Changing and remaining the same
items.example: Despite the new timetable, the evening service will remain unchanged.
items.note: Remain unchanged is a formal, concise way to say that something stays the same.

items.section: B · Changing and remaining the same
items.example: Small businesses must adapt to changing circumstances to survive.
items.note: Adapt to takes a noun phrase; changing circumstances stresses that conditions are not fixed.

items.section: B · Changing and remaining the same
items.example: The editor suggested slight changes to the introduction, not a complete rewrite.
items.note: Slight changes affect small details and contrast with radical or fundamental ones.

items.section: B · Changing and remaining the same
items.example: The new branding involved only superficial changes; the service itself stayed the same.
items.note: Superficial changes affect appearance rather than deeper structures or causes.

items.section: B · Changing and remaining the same
items.example: Consumer habits may change significantly as the city expands.
items.note: Significantly is natural with change; it describes substantial extent without necessarily implying improvement.

items.example: The former textile mill underwent a transformation into an arts centre.
items.note: Undergo a transformation highlights a substantial process of becoming different.

items.example: Traditional pottery has undergone a revival among younger craftspeople.
items.note: Undergo a revival means become active or popular again after a period of decline.

items.example: Electricity prices fluctuated wildly during the supply shortage.
items.note: Fluctuate means move up and down; wildly adds that the movements are large or unpredictable.

items.example: The quarterly report recorded a modest increase in visitor numbers.
items.note: Modest signals a relatively small rise, unlike sharp or dramatic increase.

items.example: There was a modest improvement in the accuracy of the new model.
items.note: A modest improvement represents limited positive progress rather than a breakthrough.

items.example: The fund registered a modest gain despite turbulent markets.
items.note: Gain pairs naturally with modest for a relatively small positive result.

items.example: The local economy showed a modest recovery after two weak quarters.
items.note: A modest recovery is a limited return towards a previous stronger state.

items.example: A sudden shift in investor confidence followed the unexpected announcement.
items.note: Shift often describes a change in opinion, focus, policy or direction; sudden emphasises speed.

items.example: The survey showed a dramatic shift in priorities after the floods.
items.note: A dramatic shift is large and striking, especially in opinions, trends or strategy.

items.example: Her presentation skills showed considerable improvement over the semester.
items.note: Considerable improvement indicates substantial positive development.

items.example: The new interface is usable, but there is still room for improvement.
items.note: There is room for improvement tactfully means that something could be better.

items.pt: virar vidas de cabeça para baixo
items.example: The sudden closure turned dozens of families’ lives upside down.
items.note: Turn lives upside down describes a major disruption, generally an unwanted one.

items.example: The independent cinema has moved with the times by offering online bookings.
items.note: Move with the times means keep up with changing habits, technology or expectations.

items.example: The latest figures show an increase in household spending.
items.note: Statistics and profits show an increase; the source flags have an increase as an unnatural alternative here.

items.example: The monthly figures show a decrease in water consumption.
items.note: Use show a decrease to describe what measured results indicate.

items.example: The sales chart shows an upward trend over the past six months.
items.note: Upward trend describes a general rise across a period, not necessarily uninterrupted growth.

items.example: Recent surveys show a downward trend in commuting by car.
items.note: Downward trend describes the overall direction of data towards lower values.

items.example: Demand for backup batteries increased dramatically after the outages.
items.note: Dramatically is an idiomatic intensifier for a major rise, unlike strongly in this context.

items.example: Participation increased significantly once the fee was removed.
items.note: Significantly conveys a meaningful rise; in statistics it can also have a technical sense.

units.title: Unit 52 — Stopping and starting
learningObjectives: Choose idiomatic expressions for ending activities, arrangements, access and disturbances.
Describe the beginning or triggering of events with multi-word verbs and formal alternatives.
Recognise concise newspaper-style collocations for negotiations, public reaction and reassurance.
Distinguish cancellation, interruption, completion and temporary pauses from each other.

items.example: A fallen tree brought traffic to a halt on the coastal road.
items.note: Bring traffic to a halt is used when movement stops completely, often following an incident.

items.word: call a halt to a strike
items.example: The workers agreed to call a halt to the strike after a new offer was made.
items.note: Call a halt to something means decide or demand that an ongoing action stop.

items.word: bring a meeting to a close
items.example: Several unexpected questions delayed the session until Ana brought the meeting to a close.
items.note: Bring a meeting to a close is a formal way to end a meeting or discussion.

items.example: The school introduced a confidential reporting system to put a stop to bullying.
items.note: Put a stop to is typically used when ending harmful or unwanted behaviour.

items.example: The supplier may terminate the contract if payments remain overdue.
items.note: Terminate is a formal verb for ending a contract or legal arrangement.

items.example: The council decided to abandon the policy after the public consultation.
items.note: Abandon a policy means stop pursuing an established plan, not merely postpone it.

items.example: The rescue crew had to abandon its attempt to reach the island overnight.
items.note: Abandon an attempt means give up trying to achieve something, often because success is unlikely.

items.example: The volunteers called off the search when the missing hiker returned safely.
items.note: Call off means cancel an organised activity or stop a planned operation.

items.example: Officials called off the match because the pitch was flooded.
items.note: Call off a match means cancel the sporting event before or during its scheduled course.

items.example: Police closed off the street while engineers inspected the damaged bridge.
items.note: Close off prevents access to a place or route; it is not the same as closing a shop for the day.

items.example: At a lull in the conversation, Mara quietly asked to leave.
items.note: A lull is a temporary pause or quieter period, not necessarily the end of an activity.

items.example: Aid vehicles crossed the border during a lull in the fighting.
items.note: A lull in the fighting means combat temporarily became less intense or paused.

items.example: The fishermen were already at sea when dawn broke.
items.note: Dawn breaks marks the beginning of daylight; it is a set descriptive expression.

items.example: The researchers set off on their journey before sunrise.
items.note: Set off means begin travelling; on a journey names the trip being started.

items.example: The audience broke into song after the final encore.
items.note: Break into song expresses a sudden, often spontaneous start to singing.

items.example: She broke into a run when she heard the train approaching.
items.note: Break into a run means start running suddenly, typically from walking or standing.

items.pt: a chuva começa e se prolonga
items.example: The picnic ended early when the rain set in.
items.note: Set in describes weather or a condition beginning and seeming likely to continue.

items.example: Steam from the kitchen set off the fire alarm.
items.note: Set off an alarm means cause it to activate; this differs from set off meaning begin a journey.

items.example: The authorities instigated measures to reduce illegal dumping.
items.note: Instigate measures is formal for initiating actions or a response to a problem.

items.example: The moderator made a few opening remarks before introducing the speakers.
items.note: Opening remarks are brief comments at the start of a formal event or meeting.

items.example: The delegates entered into a discussion about the proposed timetable.
items.note: Enter into a discussion is a formal way of saying become involved in discussing something.

items.example: The two companies agreed to enter into negotiations next month.
items.note: Enter into negotiations is a formal expression for beginning a negotiation process.

items.example: He broke into tears when he heard the final result.
items.note: Break into tears is a supplementary pattern for a sudden emotional reaction.

items.example: The unexplained power failure sparked fears of a wider outage.
items.note: Spark fears means cause anxiety or concern to arise, especially in news reporting.

items.example: The peace talks collapsed after the parties rejected the final proposal.
items.note: Talks collapse when negotiations end unsuccessfully; collapse is stronger than pause.

items.example: The renovation is nearing completion after two years of work.
items.note: Near completion means almost be finished, often used for building or long-running projects.

items.example: The director issued a statement to dispel rumours of a closure.
items.note: Dispel rumours means provide information that removes false beliefs or speculation.

items.example: The updated instructions helped clear up confusion about the new procedure.
items.note: Clear up confusion means make a misunderstood situation easier to understand.

items.example: The medical team explained the risks to allay patients’ fears.
items.note: Allay fears means reduce people’s worries by reassuring them.

items.example: Community leaders tried to quell unrest following the disputed result.
items.note: Quell unrest means suppress or calm public disorder; the expression is formal and common in news.

items.example: The government threatened to break diplomatic relations after the incident.
items.note: Break diplomatic relations means formally end diplomatic ties between states.

items.example: An independent test helped dispel doubts about the equipment’s safety.
items.note: Dispel doubts extends the same verb pattern to uncertainties rather than rumours.

items.example: The company published a detailed timetable to allay concerns about delays.
items.note: Allay concerns uses a natural alternative to fears in formal reassurance.

items.example: Security staff struggled to quell a riot in the overcrowded facility.
items.note: Quell a riot describes forcefully stopping a disturbance rather than merely calming concerns.

items.example: Trade talks broke down when neither side accepted the revised terms.
items.note: Break down is a common alternative to collapse for unsuccessful negotiations.
